💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that creator and UGC content is only getting bigger as a growth channel for developer tools, and right now Supabase reaches it mostly at arm's length, through agencies that own the actual relationships with creators.
  • This is a growth and marketing role first, not a DevRel or engineering-adjacent one — we're optimizing less for technical depth and more for someone outgoing enough that creators want to work with them directly, creative enough to keep testing latest formats and strategies, and operationally strong enough to run the budgets and reporting behind it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

Industry observers note that creator and UGC content is only getting bigger as a growth channel for developer tools, and right now Supabase reaches it mostly at arm's length, through agencies that own the actual relationships with creators. This role exists to change that: bring our creator/influencer program fully in-house, own those relationships directly, and grow the program into a multi-million-dollar channel. A good marker of success looks like a roster of around 50 active creators within the first year — at which point we take what worked and go find the next channel to unlock the same way.

This is a growth and marketing role first, not a DevRel or engineering-adjacent one — we're optimizing less for technical depth and more for someone outgoing enough that creators want to work with them directly, creative enough to keep testing latest formats and strategies, and operationally strong enough to run the budgets and reporting behind it. The work is currently split on an interim basis across a couple of people on the marketing team; this role is being created to own it end to end.

Source, recruit, and manage direct relationships with content creators (TikTok, Instagram, YouTube).

Design and run creator campaigns end to end.

Find and test new acquisition channels and strategies — lots of small experiments, doubling down on what works.

Operationalize and report on these programs: budgets, tracking, results.

Grow with the role: the remit could develop into owning all content from a growth perspective, beyond creators and UGC.

3+ years in growth, partnerships or creator marketing at a dev tool, SaaS or consumer tech firm.

Track record of launching channels from zero — and turning winners into repeatable programs.

Outgoing relationship-builder creators genuinely want to work with.

In a recent development, strong operator. Comfortable with spreadsheets.

Ideally already doing a version of this somewhere scrappier or more startup — someone thriving at a smaller firm is a better signal here than someone comfortable (but not standout) at a big-name platform.

It has been revealed that we hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the manufacturer. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Sources indicate that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are notable to us.

According to recent reports, once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Recent findings suggest that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

According to recent reports, we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

Guangzhou Nansha to Launch Cruise-to-Nowhere Pilot as Rollout Accelerates

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Guangzhou’s Nansha International Cruise Home Port is moving to launch a cruise-to-nowhere operation, after Guangdong provincial transport authorities said they will speed up implementation of the non-port-of-call cruise concept at the port.
  • The Guangdong Provincial Department of Transportation said it will accelerate the rollout as part of a broader push to diversify offerings in the Greater Bay Area.
  • Sources indicate that the cruise formatruns three days and two nights and targets younger travelers and families.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Guangzhou’s Nansha International Cruise Home Port is moving to launch a cruise-to-nowhere operation, after Guangdong provincial transport authorities said they will speed up implementation of the non-port-of-call cruise concept at the port.

The Guangdong Provincial Department of Transportation said it will accelerate the rollout as part of a broader push to diversify offerings in the Greater Bay Area.

Sources indicate that the cruise formatruns three days and two nights and targets younger travelers and families. It was jointly enabled by the Ministry of Transport, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, the General Administration of Customs and the National Immigration Administration.

Shanghai had launched the format first in June, with the Adora Magic City, followed by Tianjin in August, where the Tianjin Oriental’s Visio offered two sailings.

Shenzhen then debuted its pilot on October 30, when the Dream departed Shekou on a three-night sea-only voyage. Xiamen followed on November 1 with the Adora Mediterranean.

Sources indicate that nansha brings established capacity to the rollout. The port has operated for a decade since January 2016, handling nearly 500 cruise calls and clearing more than 2 million passengers. In the first quarter of 2026 it recorded 18 international calls and over 57,000 passenger movements, ranking second nationwide after Shanghai for two consecutive years.

The Adora Mediterranean previously based a winter-spring season at Nansha from December 2025 to March 2026, running 23 international.

Adora Cruises has stated it plans three further sea-only sailings in December, though those are set to depart from Shanghai on a Friday-to-Sunday weekend format.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the U.S.
    • Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals.
    • Klayman’s disbarment follows a suspension for violating numerous ethical rules in connection to representing rancher Cliven Bundy in Nevada federal court, Law360 reports.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the U.S. Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Image from Shutterstock).

    The U.S. Supreme Court disbarred conservative watchdog group Judicial Watch founder and activist Larry Klayman on Monday following his 18-month suspension issued last year by the District of Columbia Court of Appeals.

    Klayman’s disbarment follows a suspension for violating numerous ethical rules in connection to representing rancher Cliven Bundy in Nevada federal court, Law360 reports.

    Recent findings suggest that bundy had been facing a criminal case over his 2014 standoff with federal agents when Klayman, a Florida attorney, sought pro hac vice status to join Bundy’s legal team in 2016. The District of Columbia Office of Disciplinary Counsel filed a complaint against Klayman in 2018, claiming that he misled the U.S. District Court for the District of Nevada about his disciplinary status when he tried to represent Bundy. A D.C. appellate court ruling adopted the District of Columbia Bar’s findings and suspension.

    The disciplinary office alleged that Klayman also made baseless claims against the judge who denied his admission to the Nevada court.

    Klayman, in a statement to Law360 on Monday said, “The order contains no factual or legal reasoning, is subject to reconsideration and is not final. I made a compelling submission to the Supreme Court recently, and apparently, it was not considered. This will be a basis for reconsideration.”.

    • A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct.
    • In its decision Tuesday, the California Commission on Judicial Performance said Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Robert Draper “persistently violated the standards governing judicial behavior and engaged in extensive and severe misconduct.” The commission also said the judge failed to accept responsibility or show remorse for his actions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge has been removed from his position for making inappropriate racial and sexual comments and several other instances of misconduct.

    In its decision Tuesday, the California Commission on Judicial Performance said Los Angeles County Superior Court Judge Robert Draper “persistently violated the standards governing judicial behavior and engaged in extensive and severe misconduct.” The commission also said the judge failed to accept responsibility or show remorse for his actions.

    Courthouse News Service has the story.

    According to recent reports, among the charges, the commission considered Draper’s conduct during a February 2023 posttrial hearing in a sexual harassment case, where he lectured a Black attorney about Black football players and race relations in the South. It also examined comments that Draper made to female attorneys in the case—while in his chambers—about male attorneys who slept with their secretaries at his prior law firm.

    Other charges alleged that Draper made inappropriate comments to a female colleague and a female court personnel, engaged in improper ex parte communications, and improperly disclosed confidential juvenile records.

    Draper has said the charges “were contrary to all credible evidence and/or taken wholly out of context.”.

    An attorney who represented Draper didn’t respond to a request for comment from Courthouse News Service.

    Judge denies allegations he made inappropriate comments during disciplinary hearing.

    Judge’s ‘extreme and bizarre’ comments lead to ethics investigation, reversal of $10M jury verdict.

    According to recent reports, camunda is the enterprise platform for agentic orchestration, enabling organizations to coordinate AI agents, people, and systems across complex, end-to-end business processes. With built-in governance, auditability, and human oversight, Camunda gives enterprises the control they need to move AI from pilots to production — safely and at scale.     As a Senior Software Engineer, Backend on Camunda’s Distributed Systems team, you’ll help build and evolve the durable, highly available, horizontally scalable streaming platform that underpins Camunda 8’s Orchestration Cluster and powers mission‑critical processes for customers around the world.

    As part of the Distributed Systems team, you will work on technically challenging and rewarding projects, such as expanding on our multi-Raft implementation, our SWIM-based cluster membership algorithm, or high performance network and disk I/O pipelines.

    Sources indicate that at Camunda, we approach engineering in a holistic manner. As such, you will form strong partnerships with product management, design, QA, and sales, and work with your peers to not only deliver but directly influence the evolution of our platform to meet our customer’s needs.

    Curious about the kind of challenges you'll work on at Camunda? Watch this quick 30-minute talk from our engineers to learn more about the upcoming Camunda Exporter and how we’re solving complex problems at scale.

    Design, build, and maintain backend services for the distributed streaming platform that powers the foundation for Camunda 8’s orchestration capabilities, ensuring durability, high availability, and horizontal scalability.

    Lead medium‑to‑large engineering initiatives (3+ months) end‑to‑end: partner with Product to translate business problems into technical requirements, write solution designs, draft and maintain project plans, and drive timely, high‑quality delivery.

    Help mature our disaster recovery and resilience story, including implementing and evolving an online backup/restore API and contributing to improved multi‑region and multi‑tenant capabilities for our cloud offering.

    Design and implement developer and operator tooling that makes it easier to understand, troubleshoot, and safely operate a complex distributed system in production environments.

    Improve engineering effectiveness by collaborating with DevOps and other Core Application teams on CI, testing, and local development workflows to reduce PR time‑to‑merge and the overhead of working on multiple features in parallel.

    Participate in L3 support and on‑call rotations, partnering closely with Support and SRE to investigate and resolve complex, performance‑sensitive production issues, and feeding what you learn back into our product and platform.

    What You Will Bring to the Role:.

    7+ years of professional experience as a software engineer, with a strong focus on backend systems and/or distributed systems.

    Proven experience leading medium‑to‑large engineering initiatives (roughly 3+ months), breaking down ambiguous problems, writing clear solution designs and project prepares, coordinating with multiple teams, and driving predictable delivery.

    Hands‑on experience building and maintaining highly concurrent, data‑intensive software, with a deep understanding of low‑level network and disk I/O (for example, throughput, latency, backpressure, batching, and failure modes).

    Demonstrated ability to work autonomously and navigate ambiguity – you are comfortable taking on problems you haven’t solved before, breaking them down into concrete steps, and driving them to completion with minimal supervision.

    Strong communication and collaboration skills in a remote‑first environment: you tailor explanations to your audience, translate business requirements into actionable technical work with Product, and help teams reach clear, decisive outcomes with minimal churn.

    Experience building workflow automation or process orchestration software.

    Experience with distributed systems algorithms or protocols such as Raft, Paxos, SWIM, and/or CRDTs.

    Strong familiarity with the observability pillars (logging, metrics, tracing) and how to integrate observability into the development and incident lifecycle, ideally including experience with L3 support and on‑call.

    Deep knowledge of the Java Virtual Machine, especially its memory model and performance characteristics in highly concurrent, data‑intensive workloads.

    In Person Connection: We invest in meaningful face time through our Annual Kickoff (Vienna in 2025, Madrid in 2026!), team offsites, and Camundi Connection Budgets, including contributing to meetups while travelling,, and local gatherings with fellow Camundi.

    • According to a joint notice of settlement filed Tuesday in Colorado state court, Andersen and lawyer Mark L.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 11, 2026, 11:15 am CST.

    NBA player Chris “Birdman” Andersen, then of the Miami Heat, looks on before taking on the San Antonio Spurs on June 6, 2013, in Miami. (Photo by Mike Ehrmann/Getty Images).

    Former NBA player Chris “Birdman” Andersen has settled a legal malpractice lawsuit with his attorney, whom Andersen claimed failed to protect his intellectual property and ruined his in-laws’ creperie business.

    According to a joint notice of settlement filed Tuesday in Colorado state court, Andersen and lawyer Mark L. Byant reached a settlement during mediation Monday and asked the court to vacate deadlines in the case which had a trial scheduled for Dec. 7. Terms were not disclosed.

    The former player for the Denver Nuggets sued Bryant in 2024 for allegedly misappropriating his funds; allegedly failing to resolve his liability; and allegedly providing family members with negligent advice, along with the intellectual property claims.

    Andersen claims that in 2022, former NBA star Shaquille O’Neal’s production manufacturer Jersey Legends in collaboration with another production company wanted to produce a documentary about Andersen’s life and career, including his victimization in a catfishing scheme. But without Andersen’s knowledge, Bryant signed a collaboration agreement almost identical to a draft that Andersen found unacceptable, according to the complaint, “forever” restricting Andersen’s ability to participate in other projects related to his life story and the scheme.

    Andersen said he has “received zero compensation as a result of the project” that Netflix agreed to distribute.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As a Senior SecOps Engineer at Clutch, you will shape and execute our application security and cloud security posture. You will work embedded in engineering, driving secure by design practices, threat modeling, and proactive risk mitigation across our applications and cloud infrastructure. This is a hands-on role for someone who loves building secure systems and influencing security culture in a fast-paced fintech startup.

    According to recent reports, you will act as a key advisor on secure architecture. You will own the work of identifying, fixing, and preventing vulnerabilities across our services, cloud environments, tooling, and developer workflows.

    Recent findings suggest that the SecOps team is a focused group responsible for application security and cloud security across the product. We help Clutch scale securely and efficiently.

    We partner closely with product engineering to embed security throughout the SDLC.

    It has been revealed that we value pragmatism, ownership, and curiosity. We always ask: “How can we make this safer and faster?”.

    We are building a security first engineering culture that enables teams to move fast and responsibly, without slowing them down.

    Assess our application and cloud security posture, and map the highest risks across services, cloud accounts, and pipelines.

    Embed with engineering teams to review security critical features and give practical guidance on secure design.

    Integrate developer friendly security tooling (SAST, SCA, secret scanning, IaC scanning) into our CI/CD pipelines.

    Triage and remediate early vulnerabilities, and set a baseline for secure coding and cloud hardening.

    Lead the design and rollout of a Secure SDLC with actionable security gates and clear ownership at each stage.

    Establish cloud security controls, including IAM least privilege, secrets management, and logging for threat detection.

    Build internal tooling to automate threat detection, cloud posture monitoring, and vulnerability management.

    Launch an internal security playbook with incident response runbooks tailored to Clutch’s tech stack.

    Develop and maintain secure libraries and frameworks used across engineering, such as auth modules and input validators.

    Drive continuous cloud security improvements through policy as code, automated compliance checks, and drift detection.

    Build and mentor a security champion network inside engineering teams.

    Partner with developers to threat model fresh services and cloud architecture changes.

    • Partners at Weil, Gotshal & Manges have formally voted to dissolve the nearly century-old law firm.
    • Law.com reported Tuesday that 97% of the firm’s partners approved the move, which came about two weeks after the management committee recommended it Oct.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 11, 2026, 12:14 pm CST.

    In a recent development, according to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    Partners at Weil, Gotshal & Manges have formally voted to dissolve the nearly century-old law firm.

    Law.com reported Tuesday that 97% of the firm’s partners approved the move, which came about two weeks after the management committee recommended it Oct. 28. A three-person dissolution committee will oversee the firm’s dissolution, while Weil Gotshal executive chair Barry Wolf will act as a special consultant through the end of the year and longer if the wind-down runs into 2027. The firm will also utilize restructuring officers from management consulting agency AlixPartners and Davis Polk & Wardwell.

    According to Law.com, the next phase will center on paying creditors—chiefly landlords—and collecting outstanding receivables.

    Meanwhile, Law.com added that Weil Gotshal restructuring chair Matt Barr and several bankruptcy lawyers are in advanced talks to join Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, which would remove one of Weil Gotshal’s last high-performing groups. Neither Barr nor Skadden responded to Law.com’s requests for comment.

    Barr’s potential move would be the latest in a partner exodus that has helped bring down the once-venerated Wall Street firm. According to Law.com, the firm saw nearly 50 partner exits in 2026, with sources estimating at least $500 million in lost business.

    Rivals race to rescue Weil Gotshal lawyers as firm heads toward closure.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas answers questions during a visit to the University of Texas at Austin on April 15, 2026. (Photo by Eric Gay/The Associated Press).

    According to recent reports, U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas will lead an undergraduate seminar at the University of Texas at Austin on race, equality and political thought in February.

    The one-credit-hour seminar, “CIV 166 Equality and the Newly introduced Birth of Freedom,” will include two hours of lecture daily from Feb. 1 to Feb. 5, 2027, for 17 students. Sixty-five applied.

    Students will also meet with Justin Dyer, the dean of the University of Texas at Austin’s School of Civic Leadership, during the seminar, which follows American political thought from the nation’s founding through the Civil War to the present.

    Readings include the writings and speeches of Frederick Douglass, Booker T. Washington and W.E.B. Du Bois, as well as civil rights leaders the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X. The course examines how questions of race and equality show up in recent Supreme Court decisions.

    Recent findings suggest that thomas previously spoke to students and legal professionals at the University of Texas at Austin in April, making the case that the Supreme Court’s failures have stemmed from a lack of courage, not a lack of understanding, and he discussed Plessy v. Ferguson, a 1896 ruling that upheld government-enforced segregation.

    Thomas, who joined the Supreme Court in 1991, is its longest-serving current member.

    • It has been revealed that calling a judge a vulgar name is rude, but it does not amount to criminal contempt, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court recently found.
    • The criminal contempt conviction of a courtroom spectator who called a judge a vulgar name after she ruled against a motion that his acquaintance filed was recently vacated by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.
    • Recent findings suggest that basile Outlaw spent 30 days in jail after the 2022 incident involving Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that calling a judge a vulgar name is rude, but it does not amount to criminal contempt, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court recently found. (Image from Shutterstock).

    The criminal contempt conviction of a courtroom spectator who called a judge a vulgar name after she ruled against a motion that his acquaintance filed was recently vacated by the Pennsylvania Supreme Court.

    Recent findings suggest that basile Outlaw spent 30 days in jail after the 2022 incident involving Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E. Covington, Reason reports.

    “What did you say?” Covington responded to his remark, according to the article.

    “Never mind, I’m leaving,” Outlaw remarked.

    He claims that he later came back to apologize and was taken into custody, Reason reports.

    In December 2023, the Pennsylvania Superior Court upheld Outlaw’s conviction. The state supreme court reversed and vacated the conviction in late October, finding that while what Outlaw did was rude, it wasn’t enough for criminal contempt.

    The majority opinion cited an earlier finding involving a pro se party in a custody dispute calling the judge a vulgar term.

    In a recent development, here, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court also reversed a criminal contempt conviction for the party. In both cases, the state supreme court found, the outbursts amounted to momentary breaks in the proceedings, not significant disruptions.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 12, 2026, 11:16 am CST.

    According to recent reports, alina Habba Mildon at the White House in March 2025. (Photo by Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post).

    The New Jersey Office of Attorney Ethics filed a disciplinary complaint Tuesday against Alina Habba Mildon—a former personal lawyer to President Donald Trump and a former acting U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey—over her role in settling a 2021 sexual harassment dispute at the Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey, where she was a paying member.

    Reuters reported Wednesday that regulators alleged that Mildon steered a 21-year-old club employee, Alice Bianco, into a $15,000 settlement of misconduct claims against her boss.

    According to Reuters, Mildon allegedly persuaded Bianco to stop communicating with her attorney, potentially confusing Bianco into thinking that Mildon was acting as her lawyer. The complaint also alleged that Mildon undervalued the claims in a way that benefited the club and did not disclose her financial ties to it. Mildon became a personal lawyer to Trump soon afterward.

    According to recent reports, bianco later hired attorney Nancy Smith, who sued the club in 2023 and settled for $400,000. In a statement to Reuters, Smith claimed that Mildon “got ​my client to terminate her lawyer, accept a ridiculously low settlement, ​and agree to an illegal nondisclosure agreement, silencing her.”.

    Smith added that she thought that Mildon’s “numerous ethics violations in that scenario should result in disbarment.”.

    Mildon’s attorney, Kim Ringler, told Reuters that “the complaint ⁠starts a long process for resolving complications about conduct that took place more than five years ago.”.

    According to recent reports, the complaint adds to Mildon’s recent troubles. A federal judge ruled last year that her appointment as Fresh Jersey’s top federal prosecutor was unlawful. Trump also publicly called a $50 million contract that she obtained while at the Department of Justice “unacceptable,” and the New York Times reported Tuesday that she has since lost it.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The state of Oklahoma argues the rules do not let parties reopen a final judgment based on a different tribeâs case.

    (CN) â The 10th Circuit weighed Tuesday whether the Osage Nation can reopen a 15-year-old ruling that Congress ended its reservation or whether a procedural rule blocks that effort because a later Supreme Court case involved a different tribe and different laws.

    In oral arguments in Denver, Eugene Bertman, representing the Osage Nation, told the panel the lower court never finished the analysis required by the rule that lets parties seek relief from old judgments.

    It has been revealed that âThe District Court held that it held no power to grant that relief,â Bertman stated, pointing to McGirt v. Oklahoma, in which the Supreme Court said a reservation ends only if Congress clearly said so in a statute. Courts cannot decide a reservation is gone based on later population changes or other outside evidence.

    Industry observers note that âIt stopped at injunction, and it stopped at change in law,â Bertman continued. âSo it never did the rest of the analysis the rule requires. It never considered the extraordinary circumstances that only Congress has the power to diminish or disestablish reservation boundaries.â.

    It has been revealed that bertman remarked the Osage Nation is the only tribe in Oklahoma that has not received a full McGirt review of its reservation because of the continuing effect of the 2010 decision in Osage Nation v. Irby. He asked the court to wipe out only the part of that old judgment that dealt with the reservationâs boundaries and to declare that Irby no longer controls that question.

    According to recent reports, U.S. Circuit Judges Gregory A. Phillips, Michael R. Murphy and Joel M. Carson III asked whether the Nation has other ways to raise the issue. Asked why the Nation could not simply file a new lawsuit, Bertman said most cases involving the relevant federal Indian-country law are criminal cases in which the Nation is not a party. He added that the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals has already refused to revisit the question while Irby remains in place.

He noted the statehood law creates uncertainty unique to the Osage.

    Murphy, a Bill Clinton appointee, asked whether the ruleâs broad equitable powers could still apply because the case involves tribal sovereignty. Gaskins mentioned the court has already ruled a later change in the law is rarely enough to reopen a case, and creating a special exception for sovereignty issues would open the floodgates to more such requests.

    Bergman pointed out that Bennathan’s remarks starkly countered misconceptions presented by the defense attorney, Ian Winter, including that the women should have fought back, screamed or immediately reported the attack.

    “Of course, this is not the case; there are a range of ways in which people respond to the threat of an imminent sexual assault, and all of them are valid,” Bergman remarked.

    Parker noted he believed all reports in existence had been turned over and that the prosecution was ânot trying to hold anything back from Mr. Rizk.â.

    Sources indicate that chhabria ordered the government to turn over all video footage and recordings within seven days, as well as directing the U.S. Attorneyâs Office, FBI and other law enforcement offices involved in the investigation to turn over all reports created so far.

    âIf you don’t have enough people, you need to get more people on it,â the Barack Obama appointee told Parker.

    Chhabria stated that there seemed to be some pretty serious discovery violations committed, and agreed with Rizk that there were concerns with how to trace the chain of custody of certain discovery materials.

    âThe concerns Mr. Rizk is articulating are real,â he said. âRight now, we have the wiretapping charge and the government has made noise about economic espionage, working as an unregistered foreign agent, theft of trade secrets, and it sounds like that has been part of the governmentâs argument for why the defendant should remain in custody, but it seems the government has not come forward with evidence on that.â.

    • The New Mexico Judicial Compensation Commission, which recommends compensation for judges annually, approved a proposal to match judges' retirement prepares with that of state employees.
    • In a recent development, ALBUQUERQUE, N.M.
    • The commissioners unanimously approved lowering the vesting period from eight years to five years and increasing the maximum pension a judge could receive from 85% to 100% of a judge’s final average salary.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The New Mexico Judicial Compensation Commission, which recommends compensation for judges annually, approved a proposal to match judges' retirement prepares with that of state employees.

    In a recent development, ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (CN) â New Mexico judges would get a higher maximum pension and receive benefits sooner under a proposal the state’s Judicial Compensation Commission approved Tuesday. The changes would match what employees in the state’s general employee benefits proposal already receive.

    The commissioners unanimously approved lowering the vesting period from eight years to five years and increasing the maximum pension a judge could receive from 85% to 100% of a judge’s final average salary.

    The Upcoming Mexico Judicial Retirement Act and Magistrate Retirement Act establish retirement plans for judges and justices in the state, which are sub-funds administered by the Public Employees Retirement Association.

    The approved proposal puts the Judicial Retirement Act back on the path toward solvency, according to Karl Reifsteck, director of the Administrative Office of the Courts and staff to the commission.

    The judicial retirement fund has been underfunded, according to a fiscal impact report from the Legislative Finance Committee. In June 2024, the Public Employees Retirement Association reported the judicial retirement fund had $214.3 million in total liabilities and $120.2 million in total assets.

    In a report submitted to the Public Employees Retirement Association, the commission requested the association evaluate it with an increased service credit of 4%, rather than 3.25%, for judges’ first or next ten years of service. The association found the credit would not offer a solution to the Judicial Retirement Act’s solvency, and the commission scratched it.

    The removal of the increased credit requires judges and the state to pay a small amount more each year, according to Reifsteck, but it also allows the act to become solvent in 58 years. “It gets us back in the right direction,” Reifsteck stated.

    Similarly, the approved changes to the Magistrate Retirement Act push it to be solvent in 24 years, rather than 37, Reifsteck mentioned.

    Four commissioners were present at the meeting: Camille Carey, chair of the commission and dean of the University of Upcoming Mexico School of Law; Allison Block-Chavez, president of the State Bar of New Mexico; Patrick Ortiz, retired Santa Fe attorney and appointee of the Chief Justice of the state Supreme Court; and Kathryn Brack Morrow, Las Cruces attorney and appointee of the New Mexico Senate’s president pro tempore.

    HONOLULU (CN) â Three days before the Interior Department planned to put the nationâs first deep-sea mining leases up for sale, a federal judge threw out a finding that had declared the sale wouldnât likely harm endangered species.

    U.S. District Judge Jill Otake ruled Monday that the National Marine Fisheries Service violated the Endangered Species Act by reviewing only the sale of the leases and not the mining they could eventually lead to.

    âAs extinction is permanent, caution and foresight before acting are necessary,â she said.

    The Marine Minerals Administration, formed this summer by merging two offshore energy bureaus, had planned to sell the leases Thursday for two areas of seabed northeast of American Samoaâs Manuâa Islands covering more than 31 million acres.

    But the Donald Trump appointee for the District of Hawaii rejected the governmentâs interpretation of the proposed action, saying it ignored the ultimate purpose of the leases.

    âLimiting the agency action here to the lease sale and preliminary activities ignores the reality that the purpose of the leases being sold is eventually to conduct deep-sea mining,â she wrote in her 41-page order.

    The leases would initially allow companies to conduct only preliminary work, such as mapping and sampling the seabed. They could eventually allow companies to collect mineral-rich nodules from the ocean floor.

    According to recent reports, faâasao Amerika Samoa and Conservation Council for Hawaii, represented by Earthjustice, sued the fisheries service and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in August. They argued the agency didnât consider what could happen after the leases were sold.

    The review covered waters near American Samoa, Hawaii and the West Coast, an area home to several dozen species protected under the Endangered Species Act, Otake said. They include blue, fin, sei and sperm whales, sea turtles and five types of coral.

    Industry observers note that under the law, an informal review can end with a letter saying a project is unlikely to harm protected species. A formal review requires a more detailed assessment of whether the project could put those species at risk of extinction or damage the habitats they depend on.

    Industry observers note that the Marine Minerals Administration requested the quicker route, and in February the fisheries service agreed. It issued its letter 10 days after determining it had enough information to begin the consultation.

    Otake called the review âcramped, expedited, informalâ and stated it looked only at the early survey work. She called the approach “apparently unprecedented” and noted the government effectively conceded at an Oct. 30 hearing that it had no prior example.

    It has been revealed that the government argued the fisheries service only had to review the project as the Marine Minerals Administration described it. Otake disagreed, writing that a consulting agency âmay not blindly acceptâ another agencyâs description of what it intends to do. In the oil and gas leasing cases the government cited, she noted, agencies completed formal reviews that considered at least some effects after the sale.

    The government also argued that deep-sea mining is âin its nascent stages and not yet reasonably certain to occur.â Otake said that uncertainty was no excuse, because the law demands foresight.

    According to recent reports, she added that the process began with an unsolicited request from mining organization Impossible Metals Inc. The administration is ânot leasing for leasingâs sake,â she said.

    Sources indicate that the government asked Otake to leave the approval in place while the agency fixed its review. She refused, calling the error fundamental.

    âNMFS needs to do the bulk of its consultation duty for the first time,â she stated.

    Otake didnât discuss the plaintiffsâ other arguments, including one that the review missed indirect effects of early survey work.

    According to recent reports, otake’s ruling throws out the fisheries serviceâs environmental approval but does not order the Interior Department to cancel or delay Thursdayâs sale. The order leaves unclear whether the department can proceed without that approval or will take other steps before the auction.

    A second lease sale, for waters off the Northern Mariana Islands and Guam, is tentatively scheduled in December. The same lawyers are challenging that sale in a separate case.

    The groups have also filed another lawsuit challenging the administrationâs final leasing notice for the American Samoa sale.

    Representatives for the fisheries service, the Marine Minerals Administration and Earthjustice did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

    #32126. Justices dubious of fee award in eminent domain dispute about interstate pipeline

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (794 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Justices dubious of fee award in eminent domain dispute about interstate pipeline

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The argument yesterday in Hoffmann v.
    • The dispute involves the 1947 Natural Gas Act’s treatment of interstate natural-gas pipelines.
    • It has been revealed that the landowners here argue, with some support in the lower courts, that if the pipeline tech giant rather than the United States condemns the land, the pipeline company should be bound by state-law rules that require more compensation than the federal Constitution.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The argument yesterday in Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc. left little doubt about how the justices will resolve this one: they seem unlikely to hold that the gas company condemning land for a federally approved pipeline should have to pay attorneys’ fees that the United States would not have to pay if it condemned the land directly.

    The dispute involves the 1947 Natural Gas Act’s treatment of interstate natural-gas pipelines. When the federal government approves such a pipeline, the Natural Gas Act allows it to acquire the land in which to build the pipeline or leave that to the gas tech giant. In either case, if the landowner does not agree, a suit exercising the federal government’s right of eminent domain can force a transfer of the land for a “necessary right-of-way,” so long as the landowner receives the “just compensation” that the Fifth Amendment requires when property is “taken for public use.”.

    It has been revealed that the landowners here argue, with some support in the lower courts, that if the pipeline tech giant rather than the United States condemns the land, the pipeline company should be bound by state-law rules that require more compensation than the federal Constitution. In particular, North Dakota law well might require the company to pay the attorneys’ fees of the landowners.

    The justices, though, were having none of it. The air was redolent with skepticism from the moment Robert McNamara rose to press the landowners’ view. Justice Clarence Thomas started off by asking – doubtfully – whether “if the U.S. delegates its power … of eminent domain, you’re saying that it brings with it state law trappings of just compensation?” Chief Justice John Roberts quickly interjected that “it seems to me it’s just a more efficient process to have a private developer get the land under the same terms as the federal government without having to pay the attorneys’ fees that the state wants to insist on.” When McNamara stuck to his position, the chief justice eventually concluded the discussion by commenting: “I don’t understand why this isn’t an easy case.”.

    It has been revealed that it seemed for a while that several of the justices would offer a slightly different reason to reject McNamara’s argument, with Justice Sonia Sotomayor coming in promptly to press the idea that “you’re trying to separate the right to eminent domain from the right to compensation, correct?” and then pointing to “a[n] 1893 case … in which we noted, [it is] a settled principle of universal law that [they are] inseparably connected. … I don’t see how your separation of these principles honors that.”.

    For Ketanji Brown Jackson, the problem was McNamara’s assumption “that state law, with respect to just compensation is the default,” and that “it needed to be ousted by congressional expression.” But if that were true, she pointed out, why would Congress have thought it vital, in a 1946 condemnation statute adopted just one year before the Natural Gas Act, to take the trouble explicitly to import state law? That statute’s treatment of the condemnation problem appears to contrast sharply with the treatment in the Natural Gas Act just one year later. As Jackson asked pointedly: “What is [that language] doing there if … silence [by Congress means that] state law applies?” Justices Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett pressed McNamara on the same point: they took it as self-evident that the 1946 statute importing state law suggested that a 1947 statute silent on the topic calls for the application of the baseline federal rule emphasized by Thomas and Roberts.

    Recent findings suggest that you have to expect it will be pretty hard to fashion a majority if Justice Thomas and the chief justice on one side see it as an “easy case” against you and Jackson and Sotomayor on the other side are predisposed to reject what you have to say. And nothing in the remainder of the argument suggested any reason to think otherwise. The presentations of Paul Hughes (for the pipeline firm) and Zoe Jacoby (for the government) were filled for the most part with softball questions speculating about why lower courts might have found such an obvious question challenging.

    I would not be at all surprised if this was one of the very first decisions from the November session. The share of simple unanimous statutory cases is not so high as it used to be, but this has all the earmarks of a straightforward unanimous affirmance.

    Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

    Reuters reported Thursday that Gibson Dunn has confirmed that it will bring aboard a 120-lawyer private funds group from Weil Gotshal, including co-managing partner Jonathon Soler.

    According to Reuters, the group will include 23 partners across New York; Washington, D.C.; and London and is set to start at Gibson Dunn in January.

    “This is the most sought-after ​cross-border funds team in the market, and their arrival is a ⁠defining moment for our practice,” said Shukie Grossman, the global chair of Gibson Dunn’s investment funds ​practice, in a statement.

    Sources indicate that according to Reuters, several firms have started, or are the in process of, absorbing groups of lawyers from the closing firm. Kirkland & Ellis said last week 40 lawyers will join, including private equity partner Ramona Nee, who had been in line to lead Weil Gotshal and was a co-managing partner alongside Soler.

    It has been revealed that meanwhile, Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom remarked Thursday it has hired three Weil Gotshal partners, adding to the two it picked up before the dissolution. Kirkland; Latham & Watkins; Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison; Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson; and Massumi + Consoli have also unveiled or confirmed Weil Gotshal partner hires this week.

    Soler did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters.

    #32121. Trump administration brings White House ballroom battle back to Supreme Court

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1193 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump administration brings White House ballroom battle back to Supreme Court

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, once again asking the justices to intervene in its ongoing efforts to build a new White House ballroom.
    • Construction on the project began in October of last year with the demolition of the East Wing.
    • It has been revealed that to support its argument that it had a legal right to sue, known as standing, the trust submitted a declaration from Alison Hoagland, a member who lives in Washington, D.C., and mentioned that she visits the area where the White House is located approximately once per month.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court last week, once again asking the justices to intervene in its ongoing efforts to build a new White House ballroom. On Aug. 31, a divided court paused a ruling by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., that would have halted above-ground construction on the project. In a petition filed on Nov. 5, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the court to reverse the lower court’s ruling outright or to take up the case and hear oral arguments on the merits. He told the justices that their earlier ruling “has all but answered the question presented” by the dispute, and that the project “should be permitted to move forward outside the shadow of judicial superintendence.”.

    Construction on the project began in October of last year with the demolition of the East Wing. In December, the National Trust for Historic Preservation – a private nonprofit that describes itself as having “led the movement to save America’s historic places” “[f]or more than 75 years” – filed a lawsuit in federal court, seeking to block the construction until the National Capital Planning Commission and the Commission of Fine Arts could review the plans for the construction; the NCPC could approve those plans; and Congress could authorize the construction.

    It has been revealed that to support its argument that it had a legal right to sue, known as standing, the trust submitted a declaration from Alison Hoagland, a member who lives in Washington, D.C., and mentioned that she visits the area where the White House is located approximately once per month. Hoagland, who has “expertise in historic architecture,” claimed that the project caused “‘injuries’ to her ‘aesthetic, cultural, and historical interests’ because she finds the ‘scale,’ ‘height,’ and ‘massing’ of the government’s design distasteful.”.

    Senior U.S. District Judge Leon issued an order in late March that temporarily barred the construction of the ballroom above ground but allowed underground construction – of, for example, bomb shelters and bunkers – to move forward, along with any above-ground construction necessary for safety and security.

    It has been revealed that before Leon’s ruling could go into effect, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit froze it to give that court time to consider the government’s appeal. In August, a divided three-judge panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld Leon’s ruling but delayed its effective date for 14 days to allow the federal government to go to the Supreme Court.

    Writing for the majority, Judges Patricia Millett and Bradley Garcia emphasized that Congress, and only Congress, has the power “to regulate the construction and demolition of White House structures,” but it has not approved any money for the ballroom construction.

    In her dissent, Judge Neomi Rao contended (among other things) that the trust did not have a legal right to bring a lawsuit, known as standing, to try to stop the ballroom construction.

    It has been revealed that calling Leon’s ruling “extraordinary and unlawful,” the Trump administration came to the court on its interim docket on Aug. 13. Sauer asked the justices to temporarily pause Leon’s ruling, telling them that it would “halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security.” He argued that the trust lacks standing to sue, because its claims rest on a member’s “dislike” for the latest construction – which, it said, is not the kind of injury that would allow the lawsuit to go forward.

    On Aug. 21, the day that Leon’s order was scheduled to go into effect, Chief Justice John Roberts issued an administrative stay – that is, an order that kept Leon’s order on hold (and permitted construction to continue) – to give the justices additional time to consider the government’s request.

    By a vote of 5-4, the court on Aug. 31 granted the government’s application and continued the pause on Leon’s order. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the majority stressed that it was not deciding whether the project was legal. Instead, it stated, the trust likely lacks standing to challenge the project at all. The harms that Hoagland alleges, the majority wrote, are not the kind of “concrete” and specific injuries required to bring a lawsuit. Moreover, the majority said, if Leon’s order were allowed to go into effect, the government would be permanently harmed – another key criterion in determining whether to grant emergency relief. Among other things, it noted, senior government officials “attest[] that constructing something approximating the height and mass of the intended above-ground ballroom is ‘crucial’ to the security of the below-ground military installation.”.

    It has been revealed that roberts dissented, in an opinion joined by Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan, and Ketanji Brown Jackson. In his view, the construction “is likely unlawful,” and the majority’s decision was “no victory for the separation of powers.” He contended that the trust did have standing to sue because “[a] historic preservationist such as Hoagland can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys, just as,” based on prior court precedent, “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys.”.

    In its Nov. 5 petition, the Trump administration argued that “the East Wing renovation is a vital national-security effort taking place on the White House grounds with the President’s personal involvement,” and that it has “proceeded swiftly since construction began in October 2025, in keeping with the urgency of remedying the East Wing’s obsolete and vulnerable security infrastructure, all as this President faces an onslaught of assassination attempts.” Because Leon’s order blocked the project “at the behest of a single passerby who complains that she expects to dislike its ultimate design,” Sauer wrote, his “decision is demonstrably flawed.”.

    Recent findings suggest that sauer acknowledged that the court’s Aug. 31 ruling came on the interim docket and therefore “only involve[d] a preliminary look at the merits and equities” of the dispute. But, he continued, in this case “[t]here is nothing further or upcoming that this Court needs to decide after its” earlier opinion “in order to answer the question presented” by the government’s new filing – specifically, whether Leon was wrong to block “the ongoing renovation of the East Wing of the White House.” This is especially true, Sauer suggested, given the court made its Aug. 31 decision “after extensive briefing, and concern[d] detailed majority and dissenting opinions addressing” the challenges in the case.

    Sauer urged the court to summarily reverse Leon’s decision – that is, to reverse it without additional briefing or oral argument – or, at a minimum, grant review and hear oral arguments.

    In a recent development, the trust’s response to the government’s petition is currently due on Dec. 7.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Harvard Law School suspended at least 18 students’ library access for two weeks after they participated in a “study-in” supporting clinical instructors earlier in November. (Photo from Shutterstock).

    Harvard Law School suspended at least 18 students’ library access for two weeks after they participated in a “study-in” supporting clinical instructors earlier in November.

    Sources indicate that the students received emails Friday notifying them of the short-term suspension, according to a story by the Harvard Crimson. The “sit-in,” described as silent, happened Nov. 6 on the fourth floor of the library and lasted about an hour.

    It has been revealed that in an email reviewed by the Harvard Crimson, Amanda T. Watson, the assistant dean for ibrary and information services at Harvard Law School, cited students’ involvement in an “organized demonstration” in the library as the reason for the suspension.

    The email stated that the students’ physical access to the library would be suspended until Nov. 27, but they retained the ability to borrow library materials and have online access, as well as access to other Harvard libraries. The email also stated that the suspension would not be included in their disciplinary records.

    Container Engineer at Supabase

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers.
    • According to recent reports, container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of.
    • Your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth. More than 9 million developers and 250,000+ customers now build on Supabase, and the majority of new databases on the platform are created by AI app builders — so the systems underneath have to stay reliable while they grow fast.

    According to recent reports, container Engineering (ConEng) owns the internal container platform that runs Supabase's multi-tenant, multi-region services — the managed Kubernetes platform that other engineering teams build and deploy on top of. We own cluster lifecycle and cluster classes, multi-cluster and multi-region topology, capacity, scheduling, isolation and runtime safety, the higher-level platform APIs, the Kubernetes deployment contract and Argo semantics, rollout primitives, and runtime configuration and secret injection.

    Your job is to make the platform itself trustworthy, observable, and cheap to operate at scale — and to raise the reliability bar for everyone who depends on it. This is not a gatekeeper role. You'll make the reliable path the easy path: building the automation and platform APIs that let product teams run safely by default, instrumenting what we operate, and making sure that when something breaks we detect it and recover fast.

    The work spans three strength areas:.

    Tooling & ecosystem — deep knowledge of the container and orchestration landscape (Kubernetes, containerd/OCI, the CNCF ecosystem) and a clear point of view on how to compose it.

    Software engineering — designing and building the platform's automation, controllers, and internal tooling as production code, including solutions that don't come pre-shaped by an existing tool.

    Operational / SRE practice — the discipline (SLOs, error budgets, incident response, ORRs) that runs the platform at scale as a predictable one.

    Sources indicate that we expect you to be genuinely deep in at least one of these, and many of our strongest candidates are deep in two (usually leaning toward one). Bringing real strength across all three is rare and exceptional — and even then, no one is equally strong in all three at once, so you'd focus where you're most needed at any given time. Different profiles are welcome here; tell us which of these is your center of gravity.

    Regardless of the skill set, all team members carry a share of the team's on-call rota, responding to platform incidents and driving them to resolution and follow-up.

    Platform reliability & operations.

    Define SLIs/SLOs and error budgets for the container platform itself, and build error-budget policies that actually gate platform changes.

    Own the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process for fresh platform capabilities and major changes.

    Design and track metrics for platform uptime, and increase observability into the platform by capturing the right metrics, logs, and traces across the platform layers.

    Drive the incident-to-improvement pipeline: facilitate blameless postmortems, connect findings to readiness gaps, spot repeat failure patterns, and push through systemic fixes.

    Build and maintain the platform's automation, controllers, operators, and internal tooling — writing production code and shipping it, not just wiring together existing tools.

    Design and implement the platform-side CI/CD and rollout primitives that speed up platform deployments while working within proper change and release management.

    Implement and maintain security automation for the platform: intrusion detection, automated remediation, and patch management.

    Identify and quantify operational toil, and build the automation that removes it rather than just documenting it.

    Contribute to the platform's continual testing automation — the test suites and pipelines that validate platform releases are fit for purpose before they reach tenants.

    Tooling, ecosystem & architecture.

    Act as a platform reliability and architecture expert — contribute to failure-mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design for multi-tenant container workloads.

    Evaluate and evolve the platform's tooling ecosystem (orchestration, runtime, networking, isolation, and observability stack) with a clear, opinionated view on trade-offs.

    Improve system architecture to reduce infrastructure cost while balancing security, reliability, and performance across tenants.

    Guide teams building on the platform to design sustainable on-call practices for their own services: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction.

    Have 5+ years in platform engineering, container/Kubernetes platform operations, SRE, or production infrastructure, and have operated production systems at scale and carried on-call for them.

    Are genuinely deep in at least one — ideally two — of the three strength areas below (and tell us which is your center of gravity):.

    According to recent reports, tooling & ecosystem — know the container/orchestration landscape well: Kubernetes, containerd and the OCI/CRI standards, and the surrounding CNCF ecosystem (e.g. Argo CD/Argo Rollouts for GitOps and progressive delivery; Cilium/eBPF networking and the Gateway API; Karpenter/KEDA-style autoscaling; and workload-isolation runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers). You reason about trade-offs rather than reaching for defaults.

    Software engineering — write real production code (Go and/or a comparable systems language) and can build controllers, operators, and platform APIs — stepping back to the underlying problem and building the right solution when no off-the-shelf tool fits.

    Operational / SRE practice — are fluent in SLOs, error budgets, and operational KPIs; have led incident response and blameless postmortems; and have driven down MTTD/MTTR for systems you operated.

    Have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems and understand isolation as a spectrum — from namespaces, RBAC, network policies, and resource quotas through to stronger primitives such as virtual clusters (e.g. vCluster) or VM-class runtimes.

    Operate confidently on AWS (multiple accounts, IAM, VPC) and are comfortable with infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred; Terraform/CDK also fine) and Kubernetes.

    Script and automate to eliminate toil rather than absorb it.

    Communicate clearly with both infrastructure specialists and product engineers, and thrive in async, globally distributed teams.

    Are comfortable navigating ambiguity and iterating toward better systems over time.

    Experience building and operating a multi-tenant Kubernetes platform that internal teams deploy onto.

    Familiarity with policy engines (Kyverno, or OPA/Gatekeeper) and cost-attribution tooling (OpenCost/Kubecost) for per-tenant chargeback/showback.

    Experience with managed database platforms or Postgres.

    Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, Prometheus/VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling.

    We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

    Recent findings suggest that every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the tech giant. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

    Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

    It has been revealed that supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

    Once a year, the entire firm gathers in a latest city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

    It has been revealed that we operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    Sources indicate that supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

    Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F).

    In a recent development, we move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.
