    #32116. Industry News: Court appears unlikely to side with inmate in lawsuit for violation of his constitutional rights

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2098 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Court appears unlikely to side with inmate in lawsuit for violation of his constitutional rights

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Supreme Court on Monday appeared to side with a prison paramedic in a lawsuit brought by an inmate who contends that the paramedic’s failure to provide medical treatment violated his constitutional rights.
    • The inmate, Kekai Watanabe, was seriously injured in a gang-related fight while he was in a federal detention center in Hawaii.
    • Watanabe filed a lawsuit in federal court in Honolulu, alleging that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment by being deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court on Monday appeared to side with a prison paramedic in a lawsuit brought by an inmate who contends that the paramedic’s failure to provide medical treatment violated his constitutional rights. During just over 80 minutes of oral argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe, a majority of the justices seemed poised to throw out the inmate’s lawsuit, even if it wasn’t clear whether they were ready to bar such lawsuits more broadly in the future.

    The inmate, Kekai Watanabe, was seriously injured in a gang-related fight while he was in a federal detention center in Hawaii. He says that he told Francis Nielsen, a paramedic who treated him, that his pain was severe, but he received only over-the-counter pain medication and was put in solitary detention, where he remained for more than two months without seeing a specialist or going to a hospital. When Watanabe received an X-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”.

    Watanabe filed a lawsuit in federal court in Honolulu, alleging that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment by being deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs. He relied on two Supreme Court cases: the court’s 1971 decision in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, holding that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages; and its 1980 decision in Carlson v. Green, in which the court held that the estate of an inmate who died after having an asthma attack could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

    Recent findings suggest that the district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case.

    Sources indicate that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to latest contexts,” but explained that, in its view, “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

    Representing Nielsen, Lucas Walker told the justices on Monday that the Supreme Court “has repeatedly explained that Bivens claims are disfavored, that they strain the separation of powers, and that they cannot proceed if there is any reason to think that Congress might be better suited to weigh the costs and benefits of a damages remedy.”.

    But Watanabe’s “claim ... also fails under a straightforward application of this Court’s Bivens framework,” Walker continued. “There are at least three” “meaningful difference[s] between his case and Carlson.” First, Watanabe had other options besides damages – such as seeking “administrative and injunctive relief.” Second, unlike the inmate in Carlson, Watanabe did not die, which “Congress could see [as] a meaningful difference.” Third and finally, there are “special factors” at play in Watanabe’s case that were not at play in Carlson, such as the Administrative Remedy Program, a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979, and federal laws enacted after the decision, such as the Prison Litigation Reform Act, a 1996 law that requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

    Vivek Suri, an assistant to the U.S. solicitor general who argued on behalf of the federal government, told the justices that, in the view of the United States, there are “three ways in which this Court could resolve the case.” “First, it could apply its existing standards and recognize that Carlson is now obsolete. Second, it could ... explicitly overrule Carlson. And, third, it could distinguish Carlson on its facts.” He “respectfully urge[d]” the court to choose one of the first two options, “either of which would abrogate Carlson, fully resolve the” divisions among the courts of appeals “that it has created, and end the severe practical problems that it creates for prison administration.”.

    Representing Watanabe, Joshua Wesneski reiterated that “the Court’s consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade” has been “[t]his far and no further.” “‘No further,’ he said, “means we should not extend those precedents. But ‘this far’ means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach.” “Indeed,” he suggested, “to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress’s measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society’s most vulnerable members.”.

    Neither Chief Justice John Roberts nor Justice Brett Kavanaugh seemed receptive to Walker’s suggestion that the court should go ahead and overrule both Bivens and Carlson.

    Kavanaugh asked Walker how the court should handle the “fact ... that Congress has had 55 years since Bivens and 46 years since Carlson to do so and has not done so?” “It seems,” Kavanaugh continued, “like Congress, in fact, has left Bivens and Carlson where they stood ... and Congress has operated against that backdrop.”.

    Walker suggested that the Supreme Court “has not hesitated to overrule past decisions, especially those where the courts had overstepped the proper judicial role.”.

    In response to Walker’s assertion that overruling Bivens would “clear up the confusion and hand the accountability for all of this back to Congress, where it belongs,” Kavanaugh later asked whether “another way to provide clarity [would be] to simply say that courts should apply Bivens and Carlson but not extend them?” He compared such a scenario to what the Supreme Court has done in other areas of the law, such as with the Alien Tort Statute, “where we’ve had results or decisions under a methodology we wouldn’t use anymore, but we have not overruled the original three” causes of action under “the ATS, for example. We just haven’t extended them.”.

    Suri addressed this point during his time at the lectern, telling Kavanaugh that “[t]he problem ... as I see it ... is the Court’s decision” holding that “the PLRA itself gives rise to a new context,” as does “the availability of injunctive relief.” “So,” he continued, “if you’re going to honor that precedent, then this is a new context,” which would mean that “there are no viable Carlson claims anymore.”.

    For his part, Roberts noted that the federal government had “expressly” not asked the court to overrule Bivens, “and, of course, they have broad experience in this context. And I wonder,” he asked Walker, “if you have any insight into why or at least why shouldn’t we, on that question, defer to their expertise and experience on that question?”.

    Walker responded that “I think the answer is that this has been an area wrought with confusion where the lower courts have really called out for guidance.”.

    Roberts appeared unconvinced. “[O]n the other hand,” he countered, “it could be viewed as a cautious, incremental approach to such a fundamental question” to leave Bivens intact for now.

    Several justices focused on whether, if a Carlson claim was not available, an inmate in Watanabe’s shoes would still have some remedy available to him. Justice Neil Gorsuch explored whether an inmate who was the victim of medical malpractice would still be able to obtain relief in a lawsuit against the United States (rather than the individual prison official) under Federal Tort Claims Act, a 1946 law that allows private citizens to sue the federal government for (among other things) injuries caused by a federal employee.

    Gorsuch elicited from Suri that “[i]n almost all the cases that” he had “encountered, ... there is an FTCA claim brought in parallel” with the claim under Carlson – in part, Suri suggested, because the standard for prevailing is lower, qualified immunity does not apply, and “[y]ou have a defendant who’s able to pay, the United States.” Suri suggested that when an inmate does not bring both kinds of claims, it may be out of a desire to harass an individual prison official or because the inmates do not have lawyers and are instead representing themselves “and are confused about how to proceed. If this Court says there are no more Carlson claims,” he concluded, “then I think it’s more likely that they will bring FTCA claims in these cases.”.

    Recent findings suggest that justice Samuel Alito had a similar question, asking Suri “whether Bivens in this context provides anything ... of value that is not available based on other remedies.”.

    Suri responded that Carlson had rested on the idea that “the FTCA was insufficient” because it “does not provide for punitive damages.” In Bivens, he emphasized, the court faced a choice between “damages or nothing” for the plaintiff. But under the FTCA, he said, “you’re already getting damages.”.

    Recent findings suggest that wesneski pushed back on any suggestion that the FTCA, standing alone, would – as Kavanaugh put it – “provide some remedy in meritorious cases.” And there would be other potential problems as well, he posited: for example, he stated, “we know the plaintiff in Carlson v. Green would not have had a cause of action under the FTCA” under Indiana law.

    Industry observers note that justice Amy Coney Barrett also expressed concern about what relief an inmate in a situation like Watanabe’s would be able to obtain. She first pressed Walker on the question of whether an inmate could obtain a court order instructing a prison official to do (or to refrain from doing) something, even if he could not obtain money damages for the official’s past conduct. “I want to make sure,” she said to Walker, “that, in your position, there’s no doubt that someone in a prisoner’s position like this would be able to get injunctive relief against a federal officer.”.

    And she later returned to a similar topic, asking Walker to “walk me through what happens in a case where a prisoner dies as a result of medical negligence and let’s say really horrific medical negligence. What recourse,” she enquired, “does that prisoner have? Is it the FTCA?”.

    Walker assured Barrett that, even if Carlson were overruled, claims like the one she described would generally be allowed to go forward.

    Industry observers note that justices Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to be the most likely to side with Watanabe. Sotomayor contended that, “in the Westfall Act, Congress looked at Bivens and explicitly reserved those constitutional claims the Court had recognized” – specifically, “Bivens itself for unlawful entry ... without probable cause into private citizens’ homes when there was malfeasance in doing so, and in Carlson itself, which was a ... medical malpractice claim.”.

    Sources indicate that walker resisted Sotomayor’s characterization, telling Sotomayor that, “respectfully, I don’t think the Court has ever gone so far as to say that the Westfall Act ratified Bivens or Carlson. But what the Court has noted is that it does not provide any reason to extend those cases further.”.

    Industry observers note that jackson seemed to regard Watanabe’s case as, “with respect to all major indicia of sameness,” identical to Carlson. “We have the same kind of alleged violation as in Carlson,” she told Walker. “We have the same constitutional right brought under the same legal framework by the same kind of defendant who’s housed in the same kind of federal institution.”.

    By contrast, Justice Elena Kagan suggested that, at the very least, Watanabe’s case involves “factual differences.” In addition to the fact that the inmate in Carlson died, she noted that “there was a view that the prison officials had actively contributed to the injury, and ... that the prison officials knew exactly what was happening while it was happening.” “[A] different way of saying the same thing,” she added a few minutes later, “is that this looks like a pretty standard medical malpractice case, bad but standard, where the factual circumstances in Carlson look like something a good deal more than that.”.

    A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    • Alito Jr.’s upcoming book on the Constitution, the Supreme Court, and our nation catapults him into the same category once held by Justice Antonin Scalia as a leading public intellectual on the Supreme Court.
    • Sources indicate that first, it is clear that while Justice Alito is deeply attuned to precedent and Supreme Court case law, this will not get in the way of his originalism and what he sees as bad law which must be overturned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that A Book Review of Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country (2026)”.

    Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr.’s upcoming book on the Constitution, the Supreme Court, and our nation catapults him into the same category once held by Justice Antonin Scalia as a leading public intellectual on the Supreme Court. In his book, Justice Alito shares his thoughts about such subjects as originalism, textualism in statutory interpretation, the Catholic intellectual tradition, the role of judges in the United States and increasingly around the world, religious liberty in the United States, threats to the Constitution, and much more. Although there is a great deal else to be said, several things leapt out at me.

    Sources indicate that first, it is clear that while Justice Alito is deeply attuned to precedent and Supreme Court case law, this will not get in the way of his originalism and what he sees as bad law which must be overturned. Hence his vote to overrule Roe v. Wade after 49 years, Humphrey’s Executor after 91 years, or even a 128-year-old, long settled Supreme Court precedent like United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which would have ended birthright citizenship. (In saying this, I take no position myself on the birthright citizenship case – a debate I stayed out of.).

    Recent findings suggest that but Justice Alito is not simply an originalist. He also rejects the view of Professor James Bradley Thayer, and of Justices Oliver Wendell Holmes, Felix Frankfurter, William H. Rehnquist, and even at times of Justice Scalia that the Supreme Court should be judicially restrained and defer blindly to the political process. Justice Alito recognizes that judicial restraint where the Supreme Court has wrongly deferred to the political process is unconstitutional under Article III and has produced tragic results in cases like Plessy v. Ferguson, in which the court ratified Jim Crow race discrimination by the political branches of the government, or Korematsu v. United States, in which the court ratified President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s internment of over 100,000 innocent Japanese American citizens. In those cases the Supreme Court erred by not enforcing the Constitution. Yet at other times it has erred by being judicially activist as in Dred Scott v. Sanford or Lochner v. Upcoming York or Roe v. Wade. As Justice Alito teaches us, the Supreme Court should be neither judicially activist nor judicially restrained. It should uphold constitutional laws and strike down unconstitutional laws. This is what the rule of law is all about.

    Industry observers note that justice Alito is equally and rightly skeptical of the notion that judges should be Dworkinian natural rights theorists, progressive constitutionalists like Chief Justice Earl Warren, or implementers of Catholic natural law as is argued by Harvard Law School Professor Adrian Vermeule. Indeed, Justice Alito devotes a whole chapter of his book to rejecting the idea that Supreme Court justices should implement natural law. This is because Justice Alito is profoundly aware that the American people during the 237 years from 1789 to 2026 have more knowledge and are thus wiser than is one individual Supreme Court, Supreme Court justice, or academic theorist. Although he does not say this outright, Alito appears to believe that originalist judges should be guided by the four cardinal virtues: 1) practical wisdom; 2) justice; 3) courage; and 4) temperance.

    At the same time, Justice Alito is very much a Burkean. What does this mean? It calls to mind one of my favorite works of political philosophy, Friedrich Hayek’s volumes 1, 2, and 3 of Law, Legislation, and Liberty. In that masterpiece, Hayek identifies two forms of social order: planned systems of order like a firm or a military platoon, and spontaneous systems of social order like a language, the free market, or a culture of following the rule of law. No one has ever successfully planned a language, but languages have rules of grammar and a fixed meaning of words, and so a language forms what Hayek calls a spontaneous system of social order.

    According to recent reports, the Constitution and its amendments are a planned system of order, the words of which are so short and abstract that they have given rise to spontaneous systems of order around them. Thus, the freedom of speech and of the press protects thoughts in a private diary or a letter to a friend even though they are not vocal utterances or made with a printing press. Those words also protect freedom of expression in new technologies like movies, radio, television, or the internet, and they even protect expressive conduct that is not vocal at all like burning the American flag contemptuously at a protest rally.

    The advantage of a spontaneous system of order like a language, the free market, or constitutional caselaw is that it harnesses the wisdom of many individuals who are always wiser than is one judge or academic theorist. But the countervailing advantage of the Constitution being a planned system of order is that if constitutional case law drifts too far away from the wonderful Novus Ordo Seclorum blueprint of the framers, the Supreme Court may overrule such caselaw – even after a century of it having been decided. The bottom line is that in figuring out when to follow the planned order of the Constitution or the spontaneous order of constitutional case law and precedents, a justice must further draw on the four cardinal virtues mentioned earlier – practical wisdom, justice, courage, and temperance.

    Industry observers note that more controversially, Alito argues that one factor in a good constitutional or statutory interpretation is that it produces good consequences. This is contrary to what Justice Scalia used to tell me when I was his law clerk, which is that if a text he is interpreting coming in is garbage, then the decision going out will also be garbage. Justice Scalia insisted it was not his job to make the law better. This differed from the approach which Judge Robert H. Bork, who I clerked for on the D.C. Circuit, followed. Judge Bork would not rewrite the Constitution or statutes to produce good results, but if there were two equally plausible readings of legal language, Judge Bork, like Justice Alito, would go with the one that produced the best outcomes in his view. I would do the same thing.

    Industry observers note that nevertheless, in discussing Supreme Court precedents that he thinks were wrongly decided, Justice Alito can sometimes be too timid (in my opinion) in his criticisms. Perhaps that is because as a Supreme Court justice, he feels constrained in calling for the overruling of clearly incorrect precedents. For example, he criticizes Justice Scalia’s opinion in 2012’s United States v. Jones, in which the court held evidence should be suppressed which was obtained from illegally placing a GPS tracking device on a drug dealer’s car. But in his own dissent in that case Justice Alito failed to call for overruling the exclusionary rule cases on which that decision was based, even though his former boss, Attorney General Ed Meese, had publicly called for the overruling of the exclusionary rule in the 1980’s, and even though Congress passed a federal statute overruling it in the context of Miranda v. Arizona in 1968.

    Justice Alito also complains rightly about the banning of religion from the public square, but he concedes in his book that as a justice he had failed to join a Scalia dissent, which called for the complete overruling of Flast v. Cohen, an absurd standing precedent of the Warren court which gave taxpayer standing to ACLU litigants who were offended by local government Christmas and Hannukah displays or displays of the Ten Commandments. And Justice Alito quite rightly criticizes Justice Scalia’s decision weakening the free exercise clause case in Employment Division v. Smith, but he does not call for overruling it. He should do so with pride.

    According to recent reports, the argument for originalism in constitutional interpretation is the same as the argument Justice Alito makes for textualism in statutory interpretation. Legal texts, be they constitutions, statutes, contracts, wills, or Supreme Court opinions should be given their original public meaning. A judge who interpreted a Supreme Court opinion or a contract according to natural law would be violating the fundamental norms of our legal system. Originalist justices can and should follow non-originalist precedents where not doing so would be disruptive to our legal system. I thus agree with Justice Alito that the Supreme Court should follow, for example, its dormant commerce clause precedents.

    It has been revealed that there is one final area where I and Justice Alito respectfully disagree. Readers of this site, and of Justice Alito’s book, know that we have different views on same-sex marriage and Obergefell v. Hodges. In his book, Justice Alito responds to me by pointing out, among other things, that same-sex marriage was unheard of for 40,000 years of human history.

    Recent findings suggest that I will only add here that 250 years ago, on July 4, 1776, nearly every country in the world had slavery, feudalism was widely practiced, there was a caste system in India, racism and religious persecutions were the norm, women’s rights were suppressed, and the public was adamantly opposed to LGTBQ+ rights. Gordon Wood, the famous historian of the American Founding argued in his Pulitzer Prize winning book, The Radicalism of the American Revolution that July 4, 1776 was the most important day in all of human history (other than the days of the birth and death of Jesus) because the Declaration of Independence launched a “Upcoming Order of the Ages,” which helped bring millennia of human inequality to an end in Western democracies.

    It has been revealed that it is true that same-sex civil marriage is a very new idea, but so too, in the historical scale of things, is the end or attempted end of slavery, feudalism, the Hindu caste system, racism, religious persecution, and sexism. I think the sudden rise of same-sex marriage stems from the same American Revolution that began 250 years ago on July 4, 1776.

    In any event, Justice Alito is to be commended for writing an exceptionally intellectual and provocative upcoming book. The book fills the shoes of the late Justice Scalia, and I would recommend it to everyone – whether they agree with Justice Alito’s jurisprudence or not.

    In a recent development, professor Steven Gow Calabresi is the Clayton J. & Henry R. Barber Professor of Law at Northwestern Pritzker School of Law.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 16, 2026, 12:52 pm CST.

    It has been revealed that an Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report. (Image from Shutterstock).

    An Arizona judge has released a DUI suspect after not finding probable cause upon learning that the arresting officer in the case used an artificial intelligence tool to formulate the arrest report.

    Anthony Edward Rene Quidera was arrested on Oct. 29 on charges of DUI, exceeding the 65 mph speed limit and possession of an open container.

    Sources indicate that court records show that Quidera was driving his Dodge Charger over 100 mph on the interstate. The arrest report stated that the suspect’s car failed to maintain its lane and was driving on the left median shoulder. After Quidera was stopped, the trooper reported smelling alcohol on his breath.

    Sources indicate that the officer’s probable cause statement ended with the following disclosure: “This report was generated with assistance from Truleo AI. The content reflects the officer’s own observations and recollections. All facts and statements are based solely on the officer’s account,” according to coverage by ABC15 Arizona.

    According to Daniel Fenzel, the commissioner for the Maricopa County Superior Court in Arizona, he was “unable to meaningfully weigh whether the factual allegations made in the narrative (e.g., officer’s observations, signature of affiant officer) were authored, whether in whole or in part, by a generative AI.”.

    Industry observers note that fenzel’s release order stated that the court could not determine probable cause. After being released, Quidera did not show up for his Nov. 12 trial date, according to ABC15 Arizona.

    #32110. Eleven new relists in search of four votes

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4611 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Eleven new relists in search of four votes

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference.
    • The justices disposed of two repeat visitors last week, producing one winner and one loser.
    • Industry observers note that after a quiet week, the relist pipeline is suddenly gushing: The justices have served up 11 latest relists for Friday’s conference, up from four last week.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Relist Watch column examines cert petitions that the Supreme Court has “relisted” for its upcoming conference. A short explanation of relists is available here.

    First, some old business. The justices disposed of two repeat visitors last week, producing one winner and one loser. After three relists, Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown finally got the nod. The court will decide when bankruptcy courts can refuse to enforce arbitration agreements in suits alleging violations of the automatic stay. But two-time relist Clemente Properties, Inc. v. Pierluisi-Urrutia struck out: The court denied without comment the petition brought by Roberto Clemente’s family over Puerto Rico’s use of the baseball legend’s image, which raised questions about takings of intangible property and Puerto Rico’s sovereign immunity.

    Industry observers note that after a quiet week, the relist pipeline is suddenly gushing: The justices have served up 11 latest relists for Friday’s conference, up from four last week. Several come in pairs or trios, and the federal government – the court’s most successful repeat litigant – advocates review in three of them.

    The government seeks asylum – from the D.C. Circuit.

    Sources indicate that the most consequential new relist this week may be Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services. On his first day back in office, President Donald Trump issued Proclamation 10888, which suspended the entry of aliens “engaged in the invasion across the southern border” and barred those who violate the suspension from invoking provisions of the immigration laws that would let them stay, including asylum.

    Three nonprofits and 13 individuals sued. The district court certified a class of people subject to the proclamation who are or will be present in the United States. It held unlawful the proclamation’s restrictions on asylum and other statutory protections, as well as its authorization of removal procedures outside those established by Congress, and issued a classwide injunction. A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit narrowed the class definition, but affirmed. It reasoned that although asylum is discretionary, the executive cannot categorically deny covered migrants access to asylum by proclamation and informal guidance rather than through the procedures Congress prescribed. Judge Justin Walker dissented in relevant part.

    Industry observers note that the solicitor general’s petition argues that asylum is discretionary and that the president may categorically deny it to those covered by the proclamation. Requiring the government to accept applications it has already decided to reject, the government contends, serves no purpose. It also challenges the classwide injunction and the breadth of the certified class. The government argues that the ruling threatens to revive chaos at the border. Iowa and 21 other states support the petition, arguing that the decision undermines the federal duty to protect the states against invasion.

    It has been revealed that the respondents’ brief in opposition argues that Congress expressly gave noncitizens physically present in the United States the right to apply for asylum, regardless of how they entered, and that the president cannot eliminate that right by proclamation. They emphasize the absence of a circuit split and dispute the government’s claims that the policy was responsible for reducing border crossings. They call the remedial concerns fact-bound and say the government overstates the border crisis, noting that apprehensions had already fallen more than 90% from their peak before the proclamation.

    The D.C. Circuit’s mandate is stayed, leaving the asylum restrictions in place for now. The absence of a split weighs against review, but the invalidation of a major administration policy could well persuade the justices to take another trip to the border. Will the court resolve this case quickly or let it sit for a while as it decides what to do, as it has in other high-profile cases?

    According to recent reports, our first group of cases asks whether Washington may regulate private companies that run federal immigration detention centers. In GEO Group, Inc. v. Nwauzor, a class of detainees and the state sued GEO, which operates the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma under a federal contract, for not paying Washington’s minimum wage to detainees in a voluntary work program for which ICE reimburses $1 a day. GEO argues it’s not a conventional labor relationship, but just an effort to prevent the detainees from becoming restless from idleness. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit certified the question to the Washington Supreme Court, which held that the state minimum-wage law applied to the detained workers. A divided panel of the 9th Circuit then rejected GEO’s supremacy clause defenses, leaving GEO with a judgment it puts at about $37 million. Seven judges voted to rehear the case en banc, and six joined dissents, arguing that (among other things) the state law “interferes with federal immigration-detention policy” and thus directly regulates the federal government.

    Recent findings suggest that GEO argues that Washington cannot regulate a federal detention program through a contractor while exempting its own detainees from the wage law. Washington and the detainees respond that the law applies equally to every private detention contractor, whether it works for a city, the state or the federal government, and that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit applies the same test as the 9th. The detainees also note that ICE has since revised its detention standards, which they say limits the decision’s future impact.

    Industry observers note that in a court-invited amicus brief, the U.S. solicitor general recommends granting review. The government argues that the law discriminates against the federal government, because Washington exempts its own facilities while barring itself from contracting with private ones, and that federal statutes leave detainee pay to the Secretary of Homeland Security. It also notes the decision conflicts with a decision of the 3rd Circuit ruling on a New Jersey law targeting private detention contractors.

    GEO Group, Inc. v. Ferguson challenges a 2023 Washington statute regulating private civil detention facilities, which GEO says reaches its Tacoma facility alone. The district court preliminarily enjoined it, but the 9th Circuit vacated that ruling, rejecting GEO’s direct regulation and preemption claims and remanding on its discrimination claim against private contractors. GEO says Washington is micromanaging federal detention by regulating a contractor; the state says its requirements resemble those governing other civil facilities. It also points to further proceedings on remand as a reason not to intervene yet.

    A grant in Nwauzor seems likely; Ferguson presents a closer question, but at minimum it seems likely to be held if Nwauzor is granted.

    Industry observers note that two companies that went public while business was booming present a question of required disclosures in federal securities filings: How much bad news must a company reveal? Two related relists ask the justices to clarify when withholding information makes an IPO registration statement misleading under Section 11 of the Securities Act of 1933.

    In Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, the online brokerage rode the GameStop meme-stock frenzy and Dogecoin boom into its July 2021 IPO. Robinhood warned that trading might decline and provided an estimate of second-quarter revenue, but investors say it withheld information showing that trading and other business metrics were already declining. A district court dismissed their claims, but a divided panel of the 9th Circuit revived them. Robinhood’s petition argues that merely omitting material information cannot create liability unless the omission makes an affirmative statement misleading or violates a specific disclosure requirement. The investors respond that the firm’s disclosures presented a misleading picture of its performance. The U.S. solicitor general, invited to weigh in, recommends granting review on the Section 11 misleading-omissions question, but not on a separate question concerning disclosures of known trends under Item 303 of Regulation S-K (which the agency is reviewing).

    According to recent reports, in ON24, Inc. v. Leadersel Innotech ESG, a webinar-platform provider prospered as businesses moved online during the pandemic. Investors allege that the manufacturer knew before the IPO that many pandemic-era customers did not intend to renew. An unpublished 9th Circuit memorandum revived the suit. ON24 asks whether describing an unmaterialized risk as hypothetical is misleading, alleging a split with the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd and 10th Circuits, and raises two questions that overlap with Robinhood’s. ON24 argues that the court improperly required it to predict future customer cancellations; the investors respond that “the warned-of risk was already materializing.” ON24 also asks the justices either to grant its petition or hold it for Robinhood. Leadersel Innotech answers that the 9th Circuit decision is non-precedential and that the panel found the risk had already begun to materialize.

    With the solicitor general supporting review in Robinhood, a grant there looks plausible. Whether ON24 gets invited along is less certain. It seems a likelier hold.

    Industry observers note that it’s not every week that the Taliban is a respondent in the Supreme Court. That remarked, it has not responded, leaving an Afghan diplomat filing an amicus brief to oppose review – not on the Taliban’s behalf, but on behalf of the Afghan people.

    Industry observers note that when the Taliban retook Kabul in August 2021, the Treasury Department blocked billions of dollars that Da Afghanistan Bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Victims holding judgments against the Taliban sought to execute on the funds under Section 201(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which makes the blocked assets of a terrorist party and its “agency or instrumentality” subject to execution.

    In a recent development, A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit affirmed the denial of turnover. It held that an entity’s status as a terrorist organization’s instrumentality must be determined when its assets were blocked, before the Taliban installed its officials at the bank. Separately, the panel rejected other plaintiffs’ attempt at prejudgment attachment, holding that Da Afghanistan Bank enjoys sovereign immunity as the central bank of Afghanistan, which the executive continues to recognize as a foreign state. Judge Richard Sullivan dissented.

    In Havlish v. The Taliban, judgment holders challenge the blocking-date rule, alleging a conflict between the 2nd Circuit and the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 9th and 11th Circuits. They are backed by Iowa and 30 other states.

    Recent findings suggest that in Owens v. The Taliban, plaintiffs who lacked judgments when the district court ruled say the 2nd Circuit is the first court of appeals to require courts to defer to the executive on “foreign state” status, and thus “breaks with th[e] consensus” positions of the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 3rd, and 6th Circuits. Ashton v. The Taliban joins Owens in arguing that courts should not defer to the executive branch in determining whether an entity is a “foreign state” entitled to sovereign immunity, and seeks a GVR in light of this year’s decision in Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Corporación CIMEX, S.A.

    According to recent reports, as noted, no respondent has appeared. The only opposition is an amicus brief jointly filed in the three cases by Naseer Faiq, chargé d’affaires of Afghanistan’s mission to the United Nations, who says no one is presently authorized to appear for Afghanistan in U.S. courts. He argues that the facts are unlikely to recur, that there is no circuit split, and that the immunity matter affects only the petitioners’ priority among creditors. The Havlish petitioners have sought leave to respond, arguing that the legal question is likely to recur in terrorism litigation and does indeed implicate a circuit split.

    At the very least, the court will need more time to figure out what to do when the respondent seems unwilling to appear to defend the cases.

    How many places can a state declare off-limits to firearms before the Second Amendment right to carry in public becomes largely theoretical? That’s the question in Novotny v. Moore, a challenge to Maryland’s extensive restrictions on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.”.

    In a recent development, maryland prohibits licensed gun owners from carrying firearms in numerous locations, including public transportation, parks and forests, healthcare facilities, museums, stadiums, casinos, public demonstrations, and establishments serving alcohol. I thought this was America! A divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit upheld those restrictions, finding historical support for them under the Supreme Court’s decision in Fresh York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. Judge G. Steven Agee dissented as to many of the restrictions, warning that the majority had stretched the sensitive-places exception too far. The panel separately struck down Maryland’s presumptive ban on carrying firearms on private property open to the public.(After this year’s decision in Wolford v. Lopez, which struck down Hawaii’s similar private-property rule, Maryland dropped its own cert petition seeking review of that ruling.).

    Sources indicate that the gun owners’ petition argues that historical restrictions on carrying firearms in sensitive places were generally limited to locations where the government provides security, not ordinary places where people gather. Maryland responds that historical regulations support restrictions at crowded places and locations serving vulnerable populations, and contends that review is unnecessary because the lower courts largely agree on the governing principles.

    Invoking Wolford, the petitioners ask the justices to grant review or at least send the case back for reconsideration. Whether the court is ready to take on the sensitive-places doctrine so soon after Wolford remains to be seen. But reconsideration under Wolford seems like a real possibility.

    In Sprint Corp. v. Federal Communications Commission, the Commission fined Sprint $12.2 million and T-Mobile $80.1 million for failing to adequately safeguard customers’ location information shared with third-party aggregators, including by continuing to disclose the information after learning of significant security vulnerabilities. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit upheld the penalties, concluding that information about a cellphone’s location – even when no call is underway – qualifies as confidential “customer proprietary network information” under the Communications Act.

    Sources indicate that the carriers’ petition argues that the statute protects only call-location information, not all device-location data. They also contend that the FCC circumvented a statutory penalty cap by treating separate relationships with third-party companies as multiple “continuing violations,” and that the D.C. Circuit improperly deferred to the agency’s interpretation despite Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. But the carriers’ principal request is narrower: They ask the justices to send the case back in light of this year’s decision in FCC v. AT&T, which held that an FCC forfeiture order does not itself compel payment. That opinion, the carriers say, rested on a key government concession: A company can refuse to pay and contest the penalty in a subsequent enforcement proceeding with a jury. Sprint and T-Mobile say they paid under protest because the FCC’s orders demanded payment and existing precedent left them little choice. The government responds that the carriers always had the option not to pay, that they failed to preserve their claim of being misled, and that AT&T provides no reason for reconsideration. The carriers disagree.

    According to recent reports, A remand remains possible, although the government notes that the court rejected a comparable request from Verizon. For now, Sprint and T-Mobile are hoping the justices will take their call.

    How long can a “hot pursuit” stay hot after police lose sight of the suspect? That’s the question in City of North Las Vegas v. Jones, a case arising from a search for a suspected domestic abuser that ended with police entering a stranger’s backyard and shooting two dogs. The suspect was never found.

    Recent findings suggest that after officers saw a man flee over a backyard wall, the officers stated that they established a neighborhood perimeter rather than pursuing him on foot. A K-9 officer arrived about 18 minutes later, and during the ensuing search, his police dog alerted them toward a walled backyard. An officer climbed in without a warrant. Three pit bulls emerged, two of which attacked the police dog and were shot. The dogs’ owners, Genoa Jones and Cornell Tinsley, sued. The district court granted the officers qualified immunity, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed on the warrantless-entry claim, holding that the officers had not been in immediate and continuous pursuit and that circuit precedent clearly established the search’s illegality. It left intact qualified immunity for shooting the dogs. Eight judges dissented from the denial of rehearing en banc.

    The city’s petition argues that the officers never abandoned the pursuit: They say they established a perimeter and used a police dog to locate a potentially dangerous suspect. Even if the search was unlawful, the city argues, no sufficiently specific precedent clearly established that fact. It also asks the justices to hold that only Supreme Court decisions – not lower-court precedent – can clearly establish law for qualified-immunity purposes. The homeowners respond that the officers never actually established a perimeter or chased the suspect and instead just conducted a neighborhood-wide search without knowing his whereabouts.

    Industry observers note that the eight dissenting judges may help keep the petition warm. But the court closely reviews many petitions in cases where police are denied qualified immunity, and unless the error was clear enough to warrant summary reversal, the justices may let this pursuit go cold – perhaps with a dissent from denial of cert.

    #32109. Tech Report: Justices see immigration contract dispute as raising the possibility of major limits on administrative power

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1223 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Justices see immigration contract dispute as raising the possibility of major limits on administrative power

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, yesterday’s argument in Department of Labor v.
    • Recent findings suggest that the constitutional problem is how to distinguish between the judicial power that is allocated to the judicial branch (in Article III of the Constitution) and the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch (in Article II of the Constitution).
    • It has been revealed that this case presents a dispute as to whether employers under the H-2A visa program (for temporary foreign agricultural workers) gave those employees certain things they were promised before being admitted to the United States.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, yesterday’s argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards demonstrated a court open to the possibility of a major limitation on the ability of agencies to impose fines or penalties under internal adjudicative processes, at least without ready review in court.

    Recent findings suggest that the constitutional problem is how to distinguish between the judicial power that is allocated to the judicial branch (in Article III of the Constitution) and the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch (in Article II of the Constitution). The Supreme Court always has recognized that it is permissible for officials in the executive branch – who don’t have the protections (including life tenure) that Article III gives to federal judges – to resolve questions in a proceeding that looks an awful lot like the kind of trial you might see in a federal court. And it also on several occasions has invalidated schemes that seemed to the court to go too far in that direction. To pick the most famous example, the justices invalidated the initial version of the Bankruptcy Code of 1978 because it gave undue adjudicative responsibility to bankruptcy “judges” that are not protected by Article III. What the court has never done well is explain exactly how far such powers can go. Nevertheless, recent decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a great willingness to rein in the powers traditionally granted to the administrative state.

    It has been revealed that this case presents a dispute as to whether employers under the H-2A visa program (for temporary foreign agricultural workers) gave those employees certain things they were promised before being admitted to the United States. Conventionally, when the Department of Labor decided that an employer had failed to treat workers as it promised pre-admission, it imposed fines or penalties in an administrative proceeding, often handing the funds over to the employees as compensation in the nature of back pay. The question for the justices is whether Article III of the Constitution can tolerate that dispute being resolved internally by DOL employees rather than by judges in a federal court.

    In a recent development, the government sees the dispute as squarely involving two categories of so-called “public rights” for which Article I treatment is permitted: the immigration power and public benefits. The immigration power is involved because the workers were permitted to enter the country on the condition that the employer treat them as agreed; the public benefit power is involved because the right to enter is a benefit almost entirely within the discretion of the executive.

    Several of the justices found that argument rather weak. Chief Justice John Roberts, for example, commented early on that the leading case about the immigration power (Oceanic Steam Navigation v Mellor) “had to do very much with entry, a condition of entry, and loathsome diseases. This strikes me as significantly different. … You’re trying to leverage an entry several weeks, months … in the past to the particular condition of work that doesn’t seem to have much to do with the actual entry.” For the chief justice, the government was trying to “leverage what is a significant barrier to entry, where you have a lot of deference to the executive branch,” and “trying to … extend that broad authority beyond the justification for its application.” He repeatedly emphasized that the specifics of the case “look more like a condition of employment rather than … entry.”.

    In a similar vein, Justice Amy Coney Barrett stated to Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris (arguing for the government): “I think we agree that the aliens could be removed pursuant to our immigration tradition without an Article III court. But the fines, I’m wondering if they’re different. …. So I’m … wondering here why that wouldn’t be the case for the alien. If the alien violated some sort of condition on the H-2A visa, why wouldn’t the alien be entitled to an Article III court before the alien had to pay that kind of a fine?” At which point Justice Neil Gorsuch chimed in that he “thought [an earlier case had stated that] confiscating property goes to an Article III court when you’re trying to confiscate property from aliens. … I thought we decided a long time ago that you’ve got to go to an Article III court. Are … you resisting that?”.

    Justice Brett Kavanaugh pointed to yet another precedent on civil penalties: “In Tull [v. United States], we mentioned … and this is 40 years ago – a civil penalty was a type of remedy at common law that could only be enforced in courts of law. …. That’s a fairly definitive statement in our precedent. What … are we supposed to do with that?”.

    According to recent reports, that’s not to say that all of the justices sided against the government. Justice Elena Kagan, for example, found the case well within the boundaries of existing doctrine. To Harris, she commented early on: “[I]sn’t there a condition of entry here? … [T]hey wouldn’t be admitted unless the employer had promised certain things.” To Robert Johnson arguing on behalf of the employer – a different Robert Johnson, not the blues singer – she was much more pointed:.

    Sources indicate that offering a parallel perspective, Ketanji Brown Jackson emphasized that the court in numerous contexts has approved administrative adjudication of civil penalties. She repeatedly challenged Johnson to reconcile his argument with those decisions.

    But ominous for the government was some repeated questioning of Harris about “the best way for you to lose” (as Justice Sonia Sotomayor put it). From early on in the argument, even the justices who seem most likely to accept the constitutionality of the arrangement were trying to help Harris identify the least damaging way for the court to rule against her. At the beginning of her argument and throughout it, Harris emphasized to the justices that a broad ruling against her on the constitutional question would unsettle programs in a wide variety of areas, ranging from Medicare, to government contracts, to student loans, but that did not seem to make any headway for her.

    In a recent development, it is not at all clear from the argument how exactly the justices are going to come down. Clearly a significant group are considering the idea that an award of civil penalties is too far removed from the entry of the employee to be protected by the “public rights” doctrine that would protect administrative determination of the right to enter. My guess is that even those justices don’t yet know how far they would be willing to go – or how far they can go and secure five votes of agreement. I expect this case to come down late and be sharply divided.

    Recent findings suggest that correction (Nov. 15 at 6:12 p.m.): An earlier version of this article incorrectly stated that “the executive power that is allocated to the executive branch” is in “Article I of the Constitution.”.

    Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that diversity is at the heart of who we are at Xapo Bank. We’re a fully distributed team of over 160 Xapiens that work remotely from 50+ countries around the world.

    Our beginning: A world that enjoys economic freedom and wealth protection,no matter where you live or who is running your country.To achieve that, we search the world for the best people for the job. We work hard, think globally, and inspire each other to learn and grow. We are committed to changing the way things are done.

    Although we are headquartered in Gibraltar, this is a full time, 100% remote position Work from anywhere!

    Xapo's product suite has grown from a Bitcoin vault into a full member proposition: BTC and USD accounts that pay interest, a global card with Bitcoin cashback, Bitcoin-backed loans, a growing suite of BTC wealth and credit products, and access to stocks, ETFs, and stablecoins, all inside one regulated relationship.

    According to recent reports, xapo is a bank, and a bank earns on the money its members choose to hold with it. Each of those products shipped well. What hasn't yet existed is a single owner of the economics of the customer relationship: one person accountable for winning the right members, growing what they hold with us, and keeping them, and for the balance-sheet products that make that possible.

    In a recent development, the Chief Customer Officer is a newly introduced role at the top of the house, reporting to the CEO. You will run the stream that grows what members hold with Xapo, and you will own the Customer P&L, retail and institutional. It brings growth, client coverage, product management, and product design under one leader who is judged on customer contribution, the assets attracted and kept, and the members who stay.     During the 2025-26 term, the Supreme Court handed President Donald Trump defeats on two of his signature initiatives – his efforts to limit birthright citizenship and impose sweeping tariffs – as well as his initial attempt to fire Lisa Cook, a member of the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors. But those rulings do not necessarily mean the justices have seen the last of any of those complications. In the wake of the court’s decisions in each of the three cases, Trump continues to fight on, which has led (or could lead) to litigation that may reach the court again.

    In a recent development, the Democratic Party’s decisive victory in the midterm elections, which gave it a majority in both the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, could theoretically hinder Trump’s intends. However, Democrats would need not just a majority to pass legislation curbing the president’s authority but a veto-proof majority: 67 votes in the Senate and 290 in the House, which could be more difficult to obtain.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    #32100. Latest Update: The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1731 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.
    • It has been revealed that this process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known.
    • Industry observers note that first, a review of the basics.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

    It has been revealed that this process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

    Industry observers note that first, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

    According to recent reports, this process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal matter in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

    Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

    In a recent development, as noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

    Nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an important matter of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

    This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an glitch that has been turned down one or more times.

    Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

    The answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

    Sources indicate that but much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 says the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an key glitch of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

    Just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

    The cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

    And the justices rarely discuss it. In his upcoming book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

    Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

    Recent findings suggest that many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

    The clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

    Caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

    According to recent reports, question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

    According to recent reports, the number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

    Oddly, no one seems to know why.

    According to recent reports, there are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

    These interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

    Different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer new laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

    It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a company based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the issue (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

    Question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

    Recent findings suggest that the Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal complications, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

    Recent findings suggest that A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

    The process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

    Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.
